easy.q: Elder Stevenson said some of his message was meant most directly for which listeners?
options: Full-time missionaries
Primary children
New parents
easy.why: He said some of his message would be “more directly to you, children of Primary age,” and he even remembered his mother asking him to listen to just one more talk.

easy.q: What family tradition did Elder Stevenson love when he was young?
options: Buying fresh fruit from farm stands
Planting a cherry tree each spring
Baking apple pies every Sunday
easy.why: He loved his family’s tradition of buying fresh fruit from farm stands at harvest time. One stand was known for its sweet, juicy peaches.

easy.q: In Lehi’s vision, how did the fruit of the tree taste to him?
options: Sour at first, then sweeter
Plain, like everyday bread
Sweeter than anything he had tasted
easy.why: Lehi said the fruit “was most sweet, above all that I ever before tasted,” and it filled his soul with joy.

easy.q: At a devotional in South America, what did a very young Primary boy do when everyone sang “I Am a Child of God”?
options: He hid shyly behind his parents
He ran to the stand and sang every word
He led the music from his seat
easy.why: The boy got away from his parents, ran up to the stand, and sang every word “in his sweet, loud, young voice” while Elder Stevenson held him.

easy.q: What three things did Elder Stevenson invite us to do at the end of his talk?
options: Love, share, and invite
Watch, wait, and wonder
Read, write, and remember
easy.why: His invitation was simple: “love, share, and invite.” He asked us to do this with both words and actions.

medium.q: As Elder Stevenson explained Lehi’s vision, what does the tree stand for?
options: The word of God found in scripture
The Church and its members
The love of God, shown most in Jesus Christ
The families of the whole earth
medium.why: He taught that the tree stands for the love of God, including its greatest manifestations: the birth, life, and atoning sacrifice of Jesus Christ.

medium.q: Elder Stevenson said we can hold, look at, and smell a fruit, but we only know how much we like it once we taste it. What was he teaching about gospel truths?
options: They become sweet to us as we live them
They must be learned while we are young
They are simple to grasp at first sight
They mean something different to everyone
medium.why: We learn gospel truths at home, in Primary, and in the scriptures, but “They become sweet to us as we live them.” Living them is the tasting.

medium.q: According to Elder Stevenson, why does knowing we are children of Heavenly Father make us kinder to others?
options: Kindness earns us greater spiritual gifts
Others are always watching our example
We are expected to outdo those around us
Everyone around us is our brother or sister
medium.why: He said this knowledge makes us stronger and also kinder, “knowing that everyone around us is our brother or sister.”

medium.q: Elder Stevenson visited a grieving friend in Japan, a Buddhist temple priest. What truth brought his friend peace?
options: Sorrow always fades if we stay busy
His wife’s spirit was in a place of rest and peace
Friends would now visit him every week
Time alone would soon heal his sadness
medium.why: They shared that in God’s loving plan his wife’s spirit was received into the spirit world, a state of rest, happiness, and peace. His countenance changed in that moment.

medium.q: Why did Elder Stevenson remind us what Lehi wanted right after he tasted the fruit?
options: To warn that the fruit can soon be lost
To explain why Lehi left Jerusalem
To show that gospel joy makes us want loved ones to share it
To teach that families must partake together or not at all
medium.why: Lehi said, “I began to be desirous that my family should partake of it also.” Elder Stevenson asked us to consider how our own family and friends would be blessed by the fruit that blesses us.

hard.q: Elder Stevenson gave the tree and its fruit separate meanings. What does the fruit symbolize?
options: The love of God for all His children
Blessings received through the Savior’s Atonement
The word of God that leads to the tree
The joy of bringing others to the tree
hard.why: The tree is the love of God; the fruit symbolizes “blessings received through the Atonement of Jesus Christ,” including ordinances, covenants, gospel truths, and ultimately eternal life.

hard.q: When his grieving friend’s countenance changed, what did Elder Stevenson say it was like to watch?
options: Seeing the sun rise after a long night
Seeing a weary traveler arrive home
Seeing a heavy burden lifted from his back
Seeing him partake of the fruit of the tree of life
hard.why: Elder Stevenson tied the story back to Lehi’s vision: it was as if his friend partook of the fruit of the tree of life. He saw “peace for despair, joy for sadness, hope for ashes.”

hard.q: Elder Stevenson said, “This is why Jesus Christ is the strength of youth.” Which teaching, given just before, is the reason he was pointing to?
options: His Atonement is central to the great plan of happiness
His gospel is learned most easily while we are young
His Church looks to its children as its future
His Spirit is given to us when we turn eight
hard.why: He had just said, “Central to this plan is the Atonement of Jesus Christ.” Because of it, in words he then quoted, the Savior “has done everything necessary for you” to have joy in this life and forever.

hard.q: Elder Stevenson named roles of the Holy Ghost and then quoted a Primary song. Which role do the song’s words, as he quoted them, show the Spirit filling?
options: To warn us of danger
To comfort us in sorrow
To testify of truth
To stay with us always
hard.why: The song says, “The Spirit whispers this to me and tells me it is true”: that our Father lives and loves us. That is the Holy Ghost testifying, one of the roles Elder Stevenson named.

hard.q: Which situation best fits Elder Stevenson’s invitation and the promise he attached to it?
options: A youth studies alone to know more than friends
A family keeps gospel joy private to avoid awkwardness
A member waits to be asked before saying anything
A child who loves Primary songs brings a friend to sing
hard.why: He invited us to love, share, and invite with words and actions, and promised “even greater joy as loved ones around you partake as well.”
